strengths: The study addresses an important NLP safety problem with substantial breadth: 17 attacks, eight target LLMs, 16 violation categories, and eight defenses, supplemented by transfer, runtime, token-length, and longitudinal analyses.

The authors validate their automated judge against 640 responses independently labeled by three annotators, reporting Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.87 and 94.84% judge–human agreement. Distinguishing refusals, question paraphrases, and irrelevant harmful responses is useful methodological work.

Detailed results expose substantial variation across attacks, models, and violation categories. The appendix reports hardware, several implementation settings, and three experimental repetitions, providing some support for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central measurement needs stronger construct validation. The unified policy mixes content prohibitions with deployment obligations such as AI disclosure and professional oversight (Tables 8–9), while Figure 8 permits willingness or indirectly relevant content to count toward success. This does not reliably establish harmful fulfillment or violation of the target provider’s policy. High baseline rates—for example, 0.94 for AI Usage Disclosure—require qualitative auditing. Human agreement under the same rubric does not resolve this concern.

The claimed impartial comparison is insufficiently controlled (Sections 5.3–5.4). Generation Exploitation uses success on any of 50 responses, whereas other methods evaluate one response per selected prompt after their respective searches. Equating 50 prompt modifications with 500 gradient steps does not equalize target queries, auxiliary-model calls, or computation. Comparable budget curves and a repeated-sampling baseline are needed to substantiate effectiveness and efficiency rankings.

Some implementations do not support conclusions about the named methods. MasterKey’s fine-tuning procedure is replaced by GPT-4 prompt rewriting (Section 3.5, Table 10), yet its results represent the fine-tuning category. AdvPrompter’s performance is also attributed partly to the chosen small base model and distribution mismatch without configuration sensitivity analysis. These substitutions should be clearly separated from faithful method comparisons.

Important reproduction materials are missing from the manuscript: the complete 160-question dataset, benchmark code or an artifact link, the judge’s three demonstrations, and the exact 50 Generation Exploitation configurations. The demonstrations are explicitly omitted in Appendix A.4 despite being central to the reported judge accuracy. References to unspecified defaults and mutable API aliases further limit reproducibility.

The reported statistics contain an inconsistency requiring an audit. Appendix A.2 specifies means and standard deviations over three runs, but Table 2 reports LAA on GPT-3.5 as 1.00 ± 0.05. Three rates bounded by zero and one cannot produce this combination, even allowing two-decimal rounding. Per-run counts and explicit aggregation rules are needed before relying on headline results.

Table 7 supports residual vulnerability to the evaluated attacks, but practical defense comparisons remain incomplete. There is no benign-query false-positive or utility evaluation, the adaptive attack protocol is unclear, and the perplexity threshold is calibrated using the evaluation question set. Consequently, low attack success alone cannot establish a useful defense.

Several explanations exceed the evidence. Heuristic and feedback-based categories overlap conceptually, and the claim that initial seeds explain detectability lacks controlled seed ablations or controls for prompt style and defender training exposure. With only ten questions per violation category, broad category-level conclusions also need more cautious interpretation. The measurement, reporting, and reproducibility issues require substantive revision before a sound Findings recommendation.
